content_html:
Bites alone do not confirm bed bugs, so early detection depends on finding physical evidence around sleeping areas. Look for live bugs, dark fecal spots, small rusty stains, eggs, and shed skins around mattress seams, the box spring, headboard, and nearby cracks. The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) notes that low-level infestations are harder to find but much easier to manage when identified early.

Do not use bites as the only evidence

Skin reactions vary widely and can resemble mosquito bites, dermatitis, or other causes; some people do not react at all. Look for environmental evidence before assuming infestation and avoid treating the home based only on skin marks.

Inspect seams, tags, and joints near sleeping areas

With a flashlight, inspect mattress seams, the foundation, headboard, and bed joints. Look for dark marker-like spots, rusty stains, pale shed skins, and tiny eggs. Do not dismantle energized electrical outlets even though bed bugs can hide nearby.

Confirm a specimen before treatment

Carpet beetles and other insects can be mistaken for bed bugs. Safely contain a specimen or take a clear photo and compare it with reliable resources or a professional. Misidentification delays the correct response.

If signs are confirmed, limit spread while planning control

Do not move mattresses, clothing, or furniture uncontained because that can spread the infestation. Reduce clutter, launder compatible textiles as part of a control plan, and consider professional help if multiple rooms are involved or inspection is difficult.
